idiom_name: private static final ThreadLocal<T> with withInitial and remove
implementation_notes: ThreadLocal is the library realization the pattern's modern form is modelled on: a private static final ThreadLocal<T> field is the access point, get()/set() address the calling thread's copy, withInitial(Supplier) supplies the per-thread initial value lazily, and remove() drops the entry so a pooled thread does not carry it into the next task. The classic key/collection/proxy structure is replaced by the JVM's per-thread ThreadLocalMap, and the JDK itself uses the mechanism for errno-like thread state and for ThreadLocalRandom. The trade-off is lifetime: the javadoc notes that a thread holds an implicit reference to its copy as long as the thread is alive, so on JDK 25+ prefer ScopedValue for read-only request context and keep ThreadLocal for mutable per-thread scratch state.
pitfalls: Values live until the thread dies: in an application server or pooled executor an omitted remove() leaks the previous request's identity into the next request and keeps the referenced objects alive.
InheritableThreadLocal copies at thread creation only, so values set later are invisible to children, pooled executors inherit stale parents, and virtual threads inherit nothing useful.
The lazy initialiser runs once per thread and is not re-run after remove(), so state that must be fresh per task has to be set explicitly rather than left to initialValue().

variants.name: java.lang.ScopedValue (JDK 25, immutable scoped binding)
variants.implementation_notes: ScopedValue is the JDK's answer when the goal is one-way transmission of data from a caller to its callees: a binding is written once, is visible only inside the run()/call() scope, is inherited by child threads forked with StructuredTaskScope without copying, and disappears when the scope exits, so there is no remove() obligation and no unbounded lifetime (JEP 506, finalized in JDK 25). It is not a drop-in replacement for a mutable per-thread cell - the binding cannot be changed inside the scope - and the JDK intends it for the small number of values a framework passes down per request. Use it for request identity, tenant or trace context on JDK 25+; keep ThreadLocal for mutable per-thread scratch objects.
pitfalls: A scoped value is only readable inside the run()/call() scope: work that outlives the scope (background jobs, stored callbacks) must receive the value explicitly.
Inheritance works for StructuredTaskScope children; legacy executors such as ForkJoinPool cannot guarantee the child finishes before the parent leaves the scope and therefore do not inherit bindings.
Scoped values are meant to be few: the implementation caches the innermost binding per thread, and many cyclically used scoped values degrade lookup performance.
The value must be immutable by contract; mutating a bound object is possible but reintroduces exactly the far-away-write problem scoped values were introduced to remove.
